new_entities.name: High-dose omega-3 supplementation
new_entities.description: Omega-3 fatty acid supplementation at doses high enough to materially increase EPA and DHA exposure before hard training or competition.

new_entities.name: Exercise-induced muscle damage
new_entities.description: The structural and biochemical muscle disruption that follows strenuous or unaccustomed exercise.

edges.effect_quant: A 2021 meta-analysis found that omega-3 supplementation lowered indirect blood markers of muscle damage such as creatine kinase, lactate dehydrogenase, and myoglobin, but individual trials still show uneven effects on soreness, function, and performance. Newer RCTs suggest the signal is real enough to explore, but not stable enough to treat as a guaranteed recovery fix.
edges.population: healthy active adults and athletes exposed to eccentric or repeated high-intensity exercise
edges.mechanism: EPA and DHA may alter membrane composition and inflammatory signaling in ways that reduce secondary damage after hard exercise. In practice, though, biomarker improvements do not always translate neatly into better subjective recovery or preserved performance.
edges.summary: Omega-3 is one of the more defensible recovery supplements, but the cleanest interpretation is still mixed rather than strongly protective. Pooled biomarker data look encouraging, while direct trial outcomes on soreness and function remain patchier and depend on dose, timing, and the damage model used.
edges.caveats: The literature mixes acute and chronic protocols, trained and untrained participants, and different outcome priorities. A favorable creatine kinase result is not the same thing as a meaningful improvement in next-day performance.

evidence.citation: OchiE et al 2021 Food Sci Nutr
